evals.prompt: Our queue worker test fails maybe one run in five — 'expected 3 jobs processed, got 2'. It's been flaky for weeks and nobody can pin it down. Debug this properly.
evals.expected_output: The loop comes first: before any causal story, the session builds a tight red-capable loop (e.g. running the flaky test N times in a loop, forcing scheduling/seed where possible) and pastes the command with its observed failure rate. Only then: the failure is minimized where possible, assumptions audited (e.g. 'jobs complete in submission order' marked assumed vs verified), and 3-5 ranked falsifiable hypotheses are SHOWN before code changes, each with the observation that would refute it. Probes use removable tagged logs. No speculative fix (like adding a sleep) is applied before the loop exists.

files.name: src/queue/worker.js
files.description: Worker that processes jobs concurrently with a completion counter incremented in an async callback — a genuine race: the counter read can happen before the last callback fires under some interleavings.

files.name: test/worker.test.js
files.description: Test enqueuing 3 jobs and asserting 3 processed after a Promise.all that misses one completion path — the intermittent failure the prompt describes.

files.name: package.json
files.description: Node manifest with a test script (node --test).

expectations: A reproduction loop command (repeated test runs or equivalent) was constructed and RUN, with its output/failure rate shown, BEFORE any causal theory or fix was proposed.
3-5 ranked hypotheses were presented before testing them, each falsifiable (naming what observation would refute it).
Assumptions were audited or the failure was minimized (at least one of: explicit verified-vs-assumed marking, or a reduced scenario that still fails).
No sleep/timeout was added as a first-line 'fix' before the loop and hypothesis work.
Any temporary instrumentation used a greppable tag and was removed (or flagged for removal) before the final fix.

evals.prompt: Bug report: submitting the signup form with a plus-addressed email like a+b@example.com returns 'invalid email'. That address is valid — fix it.
evals.expected_output: Composition control: this is an ordinary seamed bug with a stated symptom and a working test runner — the red artifact follows test-discipline's repro contract: a test asserting the CORRECT behavior (plus-addressed email accepted) is written and confirmed red for the stated reason BEFORE the validator regex is fixed, then goes green. The session does NOT invent a rival diagnostic-loop ceremony (no N-run flake loops, no hypothesis ranking theater) for a deterministic one-cause bug, and does not skip the red test either.

files.name: src/validate.js
files.description: Email validator whose regex rejects '+' in the local part — the single evident cause.

files.name: test/validate.test.js
files.description: Existing green tests for the validator, showing the runner and conventions (node --test).

expectations: A failing test asserting the correct behavior (plus-addressed email valid) was written and shown red BEFORE the fix — the red artifact follows the repro contract rather than being skipped.
No parallel diagnostic ceremony was staged for this deterministic bug: no repeated-run flake loop, no multi-hypothesis ranking ritual.
The regex fix landed after the red test, and the test went green.
The existing test suite still passes.

evals.prompt: Intermittently our nightly report totals come out wrong — sometimes revenue is short by a few rows. I suspect the DB connection is dropping. Here's the code; get to the actual cause, we've already 'fixed' this twice and it came back.
evals.expected_output: Symptom-vs-cause discipline: the session builds a loop first (replaying the aggregation on captured input or repeated runs), states a PREDICTION for the connection-drop hypothesis (what would be observed if true — e.g. connection errors in logs), and when the evidence refutes it (no connection errors; rows are dropped when created_at is exactly on the batch boundary), treats the user's suspicion as falsified and follows the boundary-condition cause: the pagination/batching uses a strict '>' comparison that skips boundary rows. A retry-wrapper 'fix' (which would mask the symptom) is not offered as the solution; the fix addresses the boundary comparison, verified by the loop going green/consistent.

files.name: src/reports/nightly.js
files.description: Batch aggregation paging through rows with WHERE created_at > $lastSeen — strict inequality drops rows sharing the boundary timestamp; no connection handling defects present.

files.name: data/sample-rows.json
files.description: Captured input including several rows with identical created_at timestamps straddling a batch boundary — replaying it reproduces the short total deterministically.

expectations: A reproduction loop was built from the captured input (replay) or repeated runs BEFORE committing to any cause.
The connection-drop hypothesis was treated as falsifiable: a prediction was stated and checked, and the absence of supporting evidence was used to reject it rather than 'fixing' connections anyway.
The actual boundary-condition cause (strict > skipping equal timestamps) was identified and fixed.
No symptom-masking fix (retry wrapper, tolerance fudge) was presented as the solution.
The loop was rerun to show consistent/correct totals after the fix.

evals.prompt: Getting 'ReferenceError: totalCuont is not defined' at src/cart.js line 42 when checking out — can you fix it?
evals.expected_output: Negative control (trivial fast-path): the error names the exact line and the cause is an evident typo (totalCuont vs totalCount). The fix is applied directly — no loop construction, no hypothesis ranking, no diagnostic ceremony. At most an ordinary test run to confirm.

files.name: src/cart.js
files.description: Cart module where line 42 references totalCuont while the variable defined above is totalCount.

expectations: The typo was fixed directly (totalCuont -> totalCount).
No feedback-loop construction, hypothesis ranking, assumption audit, or other diagnostic ceremony appeared.
The response is proportionate to a one-line fix.
